Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

NEW YORK (CNN) -- A young man carrying what turned out to be a hairbrush died Monday night in a hail of bullets fired by New York police. Khiel Coppin's brother Joel Coppin spoke briefly with reporters saying, "We want justice." Authorities were responding to a 9-1-1 call his mother made about a "family dispute with a gun," police said. In the background of the call, played at a news conference Tuesday, 18-year-old Khiel Coppin can be heard saying, "I've got a gun, I've got a gun," New York Police Department Deputy Commissioner Paul Browne told CNN. The teen put an object under his shirt and told his mother around the time she phoned 9-1-1 that he was going to say he had a gun, said New York Police Commissioner Raymond Kelly. The teen told her, " 'I'm prepared to die,' " Kelly told reporters. When authorities arrived at the Bedford-Stuyvesant apartment, the teenager had something stuffed under his shirt and several times showed a knife to police. "Shoot me, kill me," he shouted, according to Kelly. "Come get me. I have a gun. Let's do this." Coppin ignored repeated commands to stop and get on the ground. Witnesses said the teen appeared to be holding an object underneath his shirt and pointed it at the officers. Coppin continued to approach officers, as they ordered him to stop, said Kelly. Twenty shots were fired; Coppin was struck eight times, Kelly said. "This was a terrible tragedy for Khiel's family, no doubt about it," said Kelly. But the commissioner stressed that officers reasonably believed they were about to receive fire. Kelly said the teen's mother reported he had not taken his anti-depressant and anti-psychotic medication. Police have not recovered a gun and do not believe that Coppin was armed, Kelly said. A reporter asked Kelly if it's possible the young man was goading police to shoot him, a phenomenon known commonly in law enforcement circles as suicide-by-cop. "That's certainly a possibility," said Kelly. "The boy didn't have no gun, he had a brush on him," said Andre Wildman, a neighbor who told CNN that he saw the shooting.  Listen to mother's 911 call » . Another neighbor, Wayne Holder, said police should be required to see a weapon before opening fire on a suspect. "At least see a gun before you start to discharge it," Holder said. Police "don't even have to see it, [if] they think you got one, you're going to get shot." Coppin was taken to a hospital where he was declared dead. An autopsy is scheduled for Tuesday, the medical examiner's office said. The Rev. Al Sharpton's National Action Network is expected to hold a news conference on Tuesday about the shooting. Police said they were investigating whether Coppin had a history of mental illness and whether his mother had tried to have him hospitalized earlier Monday. The shooting came a year after unarmed groom Sean Bell, 23, was killed hours before his wedding in a shooting involving New York police. In 1999, unarmed African immigrant Amadou Diallo, 22, died when police in the Bronx shot him 19 times. Bystander Dyshawn Gibson described Monday's shooting to CNN affiliate WABC-TV. "He dropped the brush," Gibson said. "He put his hands up. Police just started firing." Coppin was seen pacing around the apartment prior to the shooting, according to an initial police statement issued Monday night. "He began screaming from the window at his mother and the police," the police statement said. "At some point, the male climbed out of the window and began crossing the sidewalk toward the police." That's when police began firing, a police spokesman said. E-mail to a friend . CNN's Jennifer Rizzo, Janine Brady and Alina Cho contributed to this report. Copyright 2007 CNN. NEW YORK (CNN) — A young man carrying what was later determined to be a hairbrush died Monday night in a hail of bullets fired by New York police.

Khiel Coppin’s brother, Joel Coppin, spoke briefly with reporters, saying, “We want justice.”

Authorities were responding to a 9-1-1 call placed by Coppin’s mother regarding a “family dispute with a gun,” police said. In the background of the call, which was played at a news conference Tuesday, 18-year-old Khiel Coppin can be heard saying, “I’ve got a gun, I’ve got a gun,” New York Police Department Deputy Commissioner Paul Browne told CNN.

Coppin placed an object under his shirt and told his mother around the time she called 9-1-1 that he was going to say he had a gun, New York Police Commissioner Raymond Kelly said. According to Kelly, the teen told her, “I’m prepared to die.”

When authorities arrived at the Bedford-Stuyvesant apartment, Coppin had something concealed under his shirt and displayed a knife to police several times.

“Shoot me, kill me,” he shouted, according to Kelly. “Come get me. I have a gun. Let’s do this.”

Coppin ignored repeated commands to stop and get on the ground. Witnesses said he appeared to be holding an object beneath his shirt and pointed it at officers. He continued to approach them as they ordered him to stop, Kelly said.

Twenty shots were fired, and Coppin was struck eight times, Kelly said.

“This was a terrible tragedy for Khiel’s family, no doubt about it,” Kelly said. However, the commissioner emphasized that officers reasonably believed they were about to come under fire.

Kelly said Coppin’s mother reported that he had not taken his antidepressant and antipsychotic medication. Police have not recovered a gun and do not believe Coppin was armed, Kelly said.

Asked by a reporter whether it was possible the young man was goading police into shooting him—a phenomenon commonly known in law enforcement circles as “suicide by cop”—Kelly replied, “That’s certainly a possibility.”

“The boy didn’t have no gun, he had a brush on him,” said Andre Wildman, a neighbor who told CNN he witnessed the shooting.

Another neighbor, Wayne Holder, said police should be required to see a weapon before firing on a suspect.

“At least see a gun before you start to discharge it,” Holder said. Police “don’t even have to see it, [if] they think you got one, you’re going to get shot.”

Coppin was taken to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead. An autopsy was scheduled for Tuesday, the medical examiner’s office said.

The Rev. Al Sharpton’s National Action Network was expected to hold a news conference Tuesday about the shooting.

Police said they were investigating whether Coppin had a history of mental illness and whether his mother had tried to have him hospitalized earlier Monday.

The shooting occurred a year after Sean Bell, 23, an unarmed groom, was killed hours before his wedding in a shooting involving New York police. In 1999, Amadou Diallo, a 22-year-old unarmed African immigrant, died after police in the Bronx shot him 19 times.

Bystander Dyshawn Gibson described Monday’s shooting to CNN affiliate WABC-TV.

“He dropped the brush,” Gibson said. “He put his hands up. Police just started firing.”

According to an initial police statement issued Monday night, Coppin had been seen pacing around the apartment before the shooting.

“He began screaming from the window at his mother and the police,” the statement said. “At some point, the male climbed out of the window and began crossing the sidewalk toward the police.”

That is when officers opened fire, a police spokesman said.

New York Police Commissioner Raymond Kelly said Coppin had placed an item beneath his shirt and, around the time his mother made the emergency call, told her he intended to claim he had a gun. Kelly said the teenager told his mother, “I’m prepared to die.”

When officers reached the Bedford-Stuyvesant apartment, Kelly said, Coppin had something tucked under his shirt and repeatedly displayed a knife to police. According to Kelly, Coppin yelled, “Shoot me, kill me,” along with, “Come get me. I have a gun. Let’s do this.”

Kelly said Coppin did not obey repeated police orders to stop and lie on the ground. Witnesses reported that he seemed to be holding something under his shirt and aiming it toward officers. Kelly said Coppin kept moving toward police as they continued telling him to stop.

Officers fired 20 rounds, striking Coppin eight times, Kelly said.

“This was a terrible tragedy for Khiel’s family, no doubt about it,” Kelly said. However, he emphasized that the officers had reasonable grounds to believe they were about to be shot.

Kelly also said Coppin’s mother told police that her son had not taken his prescribed antidepressant and antipsychotic medication. No gun was found, and police do not believe Coppin was armed, Kelly said.

When a reporter asked whether Coppin might have been trying to provoke police into shooting him, a situation commonly referred to in law enforcement as “suicide by cop,” Kelly answered, “That’s certainly a possibility.”

Andre Wildman, a neighbor who told CNN he witnessed the shooting, said, “The boy didn’t have no gun, he had a brush on him.”

Another neighbor, Wayne Holder, said he believed police should have to actually see a weapon before firing at a suspect. “At least see a gun before you start to discharge it,” Holder said. He added that police “don’t even have to see it, [if] they think you got one, you’re going to get shot.”

Coppin was transported to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead. The medical examiner’s office said an autopsy was planned for Tuesday.

The Rev. Al Sharpton’s National Action Network was expected to hold a Tuesday news conference regarding the shooting.

Police said they were looking into whether Coppin had a history of mental illness and whether his mother had attempted to have him admitted to a hospital earlier on Monday.

The shooting occurred one year after Sean Bell, a 23-year-old unarmed groom, was killed by New York police hours before his wedding. In 1999, Amadou Diallo, a 22-year-old unarmed African immigrant, was killed after police in the Bronx shot him 19 times.

Dyshawn Gibson, a bystander, described Monday’s shooting to CNN affiliate WABC-TV. “He dropped the brush,” Gibson said. “He put his hands up. Police just started firing.”

According to an initial police statement released Monday night, Coppin had been seen walking back and forth inside the apartment before the shooting. “He began screaming from the window at his mother and the police,” the statement said. “At some point, the male climbed out of the window and began crossing the sidewalk toward the police.”

A police spokesman said officers opened fire at that point.

CNN’s Jennifer Rizzo, Janine Brady and Alina Cho contributed to the report. The Associated Press also contributed.

Police identified the teen as **Khiel Coppin**, who was killed outside his family’s home in the Bedford-Stuyvesant section of Brooklyn after a confrontation with officers.

When police arrived, Coppin allegedly emerged from the home and moved toward officers while holding an object under or near his clothing.

Officers opened fire, striking him multiple times, police said. Investigators later determined the object was not a firearm but a **hairbrush**.

Relatives said Coppin had struggled with emotional or mental health issues, according to local reports at the time, and questioned why the encounter ended in his death.

Police officials said the officers believed they faced an imminent threat. The department said the shooting would be reviewed internally, as is standard in police-involved shootings, and the Brooklyn district attorney’s office was expected to examine the case.

The killing came at a time of heightened scrutiny of the NYPD’s use of deadly force, particularly in communities of color. Just a year earlier, the fatal police shooting of Sean Bell in Queens had sparked widespread protests and renewed debate over police tactics.

Community advocates said Coppin’s death underscored the need for better crisis-response training, especially in situations involving people who may be in emotional distress.

“This is every parent’s nightmare,” one community member said near the scene. “A young man is dead, and the weapon turned out not to be a weapon at all.”
